prompt: How many distinct permutations of the letters of the word REDDER are there that do not contain a palindromic substring of length at least two? (A *substring* is a contiguous block of letters that is part of the string. A string is *palindromic* if it is the same when read backwards.)

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
Two equal letters that are adjacent, or separated by a single letter, give a palindromic substring of length $2$ or $3$. So any three consecutive letters must be distinct. If the word starts $XYZ$ (three distinct letters from $R,E,D$), the fourth letter must differ from $Y,Z$, so it is $X$; then the fifth is $Y$ and the sixth is $Z$. So the word has the form $XYZXYZ$, which indeed has no palindromic substring. There are $3!=6$ choices of $(X,Y,Z)$.

**Answer: 6**

prompt: Your math friend Steven rolls five fair icosahedral dice (each of which is labelled $1,2,\dots,20$ on its sides). He conceals the results but tells you that at least half of the rolls are $20$. Suspicious, you examine the first two dice and find that they show $20$ and $19$ in that order. Assuming that Steven is truthful, what is the probability that all three remaining concealed dice show $20$?

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
Given the first two dice are $20$ and $19$, the statement "at least half of the rolls are $20$" (at least $3$ of $5$) means at least two of the last three dice show $20$. All three show $20$ in $1$ way; exactly two show $20$ in $3\cdot19=57$ ways (the other die is one of the $19$ non-$20$ values). All such outcomes are equally likely, so the probability is $\frac1{1+57}=\frac1{58}$.

**Answer: $\frac1{58}$**

prompt: Reimu and Sanae play a game using $4$ fair coins. Initially both sides of each coin are white. Starting with Reimu, they take turns to color one of the white sides either red or green. After all sides are colored, the $4$ coins are tossed. If there are more red sides showing up, then Reimu wins, and if there are more green sides showing up, then Sanae wins. However, if there is an equal number of red sides and green sides, then neither of them wins. Given that both of them play optimally to maximize the probability of winning, what is the probability that Reimu wins?

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
Coloring a side with your own color never hurts you, so Reimu always colors red and Sanae always colors green. In any final position the number of red-red coins equals the number of green-green coins (equal numbers of red and green sides in total), so by symmetry Reimu and Sanae win with the same probability. Hence each maximizes her winning chance by minimizing the probability of a tie, i.e. both want the same thing.

The tie probability is smallest when every coin has one red and one green side (then the number of red sides showing is $\mathrm{Bin}(4,\tfrac12)$ and a tie needs exactly $2$ reds). This is achievable: Reimu colors a side of a fresh coin red and Sanae colors the opposite side green. Then $P(\text{tie})=\binom42/16=\frac38$, and Reimu wins with probability $\frac{1-3/8}{2}=\frac5{16}$ (equivalently $\frac{\binom43+\binom44}{16}$).

**Answer: $\frac5{16}$**

prompt: Yannick is playing a game with $100$ rounds, starting with $1$ coin. During each round, there is an $n\%$ chance that he gains an extra coin, where $n$ is the number of coins he has at the beginning of the round. What is the expected number of coins he will have at the end of the game?

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
Let $X_i$ be the number of coins after round $i$ (it never exceeds $101$, so the percentage is always at most $100\%$). Given $X_{i-1}=x$, the number of coins increases by $1$ with probability $\frac x{100}$. So $E[X_i\mid X_{i-1}=x]=x+\frac x{100}=1.01x$. Taking expectations, $E[X_i]=1.01\,E[X_{i-1}]$, hence $E[X_{100}]=1.01^{100}$.

**Answer: $1.01^{100}$**

prompt: Contessa is taking a random lattice walk in the plane, starting at $(1,1)$. (In a random lattice walk, one moves up, down, left, or right $1$ unit with equal probability at each step.) If she lands on a point of the form $(6m,6n)$ for $m,n\in\mathbb Z$, she ascends to heaven, but if she lands on a point of the form $(6m+3,6n+3)$ for $m,n\in\mathbb Z$, she descends to hell. What is the probability that she ascends to heaven?

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
Let $P(m,n)$ be the probability of reaching heaven from $(m,n)$. Then $P=1$ at $(6a,6b)$, $P=0$ at $(6a+3,6b+3)$, and elsewhere $P$ is the average of its four neighbours. By uniqueness we may use symmetries: $P(m,n)=P(m+6a,n+6b)=P(n,m)=P(-m,n)$, and $P(m,n)=1-P(m+3,n+3)$ (swap heaven and hell).

For example $P(1,2)=P(-1,-2)=1-P(2,1)=1-P(1,2)$, so $P(1,2)=\frac12$. The averaging equations at $(1,1)$, $(0,1)$, $(0,2)$ give
$$4P(1,1)=2P(0,1)+1,\quad 4P(0,1)=P(0,2)+2P(1,1)+1,\quad 4P(0,2)=P(0,1)+\tfrac32.$$
Solving: $P(1,1)=\frac{13}{22}$.

**Answer: $\frac{13}{22}$**

prompt: A point $P$ lies at the center of square $ABCD$. A sequence of points $\{P_n\}$ is determined by $P_0=P$, and given point $P_i$, point $P_{i+1}$ is obtained by reflecting $P_i$ over one of the four lines $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DA$, chosen uniformly at random and independently for each $i$. What is the probability that $P_8=P$?

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
Place $P_0$ at the origin and the lines at $x=\pm\frac12$, $y=\pm\frac12$. Reflections tile the plane, so consider the images of $P$: they are lattice points. Reflect all points with even $x$-coordinate across the $y$-axis and all points with even $y$-coordinate across the $x$-axis; each coordinate is then rearranged along $\dots,4,-3,2,-1,0,1,-2,3,-4,\dots$ and a reflection across one of the lines becomes a unit step in one coordinate direction (up, down, left or right). So $P_8=P$ iff a random lattice walk of $8$ steps returns to the origin.

Such a walk needs equally many up/down and left/right steps. Rotating by $45^\circ$, a step is determined by two independent choices (is it "left or up", is it "right or up"), and returning to the origin means exactly $4$ of the $8$ steps are of each of these two kinds, chosen independently: $\binom84^2=4900$ walks out of $4^8=65536$. So the probability is $\frac{4900}{65536}=\frac{1225}{16384}$.

**Answer: $\frac{1225}{16384}$**

prompt:
In an election for the Peer Pressure High School student council president, there are $2019$ voters and two candidates Alice and Celia (who are voters themselves). At the beginning, Alice and Celia both vote for themselves, and Alice's boyfriend Bob votes for Alice as well. Then one by one, each of the remaining $2016$ voters votes for a candidate randomly, with probabilities proportional to the current number of the respective candidate's votes. For example, the first undecided voter David has a $\frac23$ probability of voting for Alice and a $\frac13$ probability of voting for Celia.

What is the probability that Alice wins the election (by having more votes than Celia)?

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
Let $P_n(m)$ be the probability that after $n$ voters have voted (including Alice, Celia, Bob), Alice has $m$ votes. We claim that for $n\ge3$, the values $P_n(2),P_n(3),\dots,P_n(n-1)$ are in ratio $1:2:\dots:(n-2)$, i.e. $P_n(m)$ is proportional to $m-1$. For $n=3$ only $m=2$ occurs, and the claim is trivial; in the inductive step
$$P_{k+1}(i)=\frac{k-i}{k}P_k(i)+\frac{i-1}{k}P_k(i-1)\ \propto\ (k-i)(i-1)+(i-1)(i-2)=(i-1)(k-2)\ \propto\ i-1,$$
which proves the claim (the boundary cases $i=2,k$ are checked directly).

With $n=2019$, $P(m)\propto m-1$ for $m=2,\dots,2018$. Celia wins iff Alice has at most $1009$ votes ($2019$ is odd, so no ties): weights $1+2+\dots+1008=\frac{1008\cdot1009}2$, out of $1+\dots+2017=\frac{2017\cdot2018}2$. So $P(\text{Celia})=\frac{1008\cdot1009}{2017\cdot2018}=\frac{504}{2017}$ and Alice wins with probability $\frac{1513}{2017}$.

**Answer: $\frac{1513}{2017}$**

prompt: For a positive integer $N$, we color the positive divisors of $N$ (including $1$ and $N$) with four colors. A coloring is called *multichromatic* if whenever $a$, $b$ and $\gcd(a,b)$ are pairwise distinct divisors of $N$, then they have pairwise distinct colors. What is the maximum possible number of multichromatic colorings a positive integer can have if it is not the power of any prime?

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
Triples $(a,b,\gcd(a,b))$ of distinct divisors must be rainbow. Three or more constraints force five colors in these cases, which is impossible with four colors:
- $pqr\mid N$ (three distinct primes): $(p,q,1),(p,r,1),(q,r,1)$ force $p,q,r,1$ to have four distinct colors, and $(pq,r,1)$, $(pq,pr,p)$, $(pq,qr,q)$ then force $pq$ to avoid all four.
- $p^3q\mid N$: the triples $(p^i,q,1)$ and $(p^i,p^jq,p^j)$ force $1,q,p,p^2,p^3$ to be pairwise distinct (five colors).
- $p^2q^2\mid N$: $1,p,q,p^2,q^2$ must be pairwise distinct (five colors).

Every non-prime-power $N$ other than $pq$ and $p^2q$ (up to naming the primes) is divisible by $pqr$, $p^3q$ or $p^2q^2$, so $N=pq$ or $N=p^2q$.
- $N=pq$: only $(p,q,1)$ matters: $4\cdot3\cdot2=24$ ways, and $pq$ is free: $\times4$, total $96$.
- $N=p^2q$: the triples $(p,q,1)$, $(p^2,q,1)$, $(p^2,pq,p)$ force $1,p,q,p^2$ to be four distinct colors ($24$ ways), $pq$ must differ from $p$ and $p^2$ ($2$ ways), and $p^2q$ is free ($4$ ways): $24\cdot2\cdot4=192$.

The maximum is $192$.

**Answer: 192**

prompt: How many ways can one fill a $3\times3$ square grid with nonnegative integers such that no *nonzero* integer appears more than once in the same row or column and the sum of the numbers in every row and column equals $7$?

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
A row of three nonnegative integers with sum $7$ and no repeated nonzero value is one of $(0,0,7)$, $(0,1,6)$, $(0,2,5)$, $(0,3,4)$, $(1,2,4)$ up to order. In each case, writing the entries in binary, exactly one entry has a $1$ in the units place, exactly one has a $1$ in the $2$'s place and exactly one has a $1$ in the $4$'s place. Conversely any three numbers with this property have distinct binary supports and sum $1+2+4=7$.

So a valid grid corresponds to: choose three cells to receive $1$, no two in the same row/column (a permutation matrix); likewise for $2$ and for $4$; then add. Each row and column then gets exactly one of each power of two, so the sums are $7$ and no nonzero value repeats in a line (the values in a line have disjoint binary supports). This gives a bijection, so the count is $(3!)^3=216$.

**Answer: 216**

prompt: Fred the Four-Dimensional Fluffy Sheep is walking in $4$-dimensional space. He starts at the origin. Each minute, he walks from his current position $(a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4)$ to some position $(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)$ with integer coordinates satisfying $$(x_1-a_1)^2+(x_2-a_2)^2+(x_3-a_3)^2+(x_4-a_4)^2=4\quad\text{and}\quad|(x_1+x_2+x_3+x_4)-(a_1+a_2+a_3+a_4)|=2.$$ In how many ways can Fred reach $(10,10,10,10)$ after exactly $40$ minutes, if he is allowed to pass through this point during his walk?

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
The possible steps are $\pm(2,0,0,0)$, $\pm(1,1,1,-1)$ and their permutations: these $16$ vectors are the vertices of a $4$-dimensional cube. Change coordinates to
$$\left(\tfrac{x_1+x_2+x_3+x_4}2,\ \tfrac{x_1+x_2-x_3-x_4}2,\ \tfrac{x_1-x_2+x_3-x_4}2,\ \tfrac{x_1-x_2-x_3+x_4}2\right).$$
The steps become all sixteen vectors $\langle\pm1,\pm1,\pm1,\pm1\rangle$, i.e. each new coordinate independently changes by $\pm1$, and the target $(10,10,10,10)$ becomes $(20,0,0,0)$.

In $40$ steps the first coordinate must go up $30$ times and down $10$ times ($\binom{40}{10}$ ways), and each of the other three coordinates up $20$ and down $20$ times ($\binom{40}{20}$ ways each). The count is $\binom{40}{10}\binom{40}{20}^3$.

**Answer: $\binom{40}{10}\binom{40}{20}^3$**
